title: Sampling from Your Language Model One Byte at a Time
claim: Standard generation from a prompt ending mid-token yields broken continuations; our byte-level sampler recovers the correct continuation across languages.
layout: 1 panel, three stacked code-terminal examples, top-to-bottom, red ✗ vs green ✓ marks
description: A single rounded gray terminal-style box holds three stacked REPL examples. Each example shows a baseline call, such as olmo.generate(tok.encode(...)) or qwen.generate(...), followed by its output in quotes with a red ✗. Below it is a ByteSampler call on the same prompt, with its output and a green ✔. Example 1 is English, with a prompt ending in a partial word, 'This a tes'. The baseline outputs the nonsense 'erstor' and ByteSampler outputs 't'. Example 2 is Chinese, 'Japan's capital is Tokyo, China's capital', with small English glosses above the text. The baseline outputs 'also is Beijing' and ByteSampler outputs 'is Beijing'. Example 3 is code, 'document.getElement'. The baseline outputs "('div')" and ByteSampler outputs "ById('button')". Code is in monospace and prompts are in blue. The red and green marks draw the eye first.
caption: ByteSampler resolves the prompt boundary problem (exhibited in the output of generate()). In this example, test, 都是, and .getElementById are all single tokens in the respective tokenizers.
abstract: Tokenization is used almost universally by modern language models, enabling efficient text representation using multi-byte or multi-character tokens. However, prior work has shown that tokenization can introduce distortion into the model's generations, an issue known as the Prompt Boundary Problem (PBP). For example, users are often advised not to end their prompts with a space because it prevents the model from including the space as part of the next token. While this heuristic is effective in English, the underlying PBP continues to affect code generation and languages such as Chinese, where tokens often do not line up with word and syntactic boundaries. In this work, we present an inference-time method to convert any autoregressive LM with a BPE tokenizer into a character-level or byte-level LM. Our method efficiently solves the PBP and is also able to unify the vocabularies of language models with different tokenizers, allowing one to ensemble LMs with different tokenizers at inference time or transfer the post-training from one model to another using proxy-tuning. Code is available at https://github.com/SewoongLab/byte-sampler .
